decisions.rationale: Post-flight wear/condition inspection is explicitly source-defined at a different lifecycle phase from preflight inspection and scheduled maintenance.
The source explicitly lists abnormal equipment heating as a post-flight inspection item. The C002 reconciliation to Tier A is appropriate; no controlled-variant claim is needed.
Operation-end safe storage plus flight-log creation is explicitly source-defined as an end-of-day process and differs from questions that test only statutory log contents or carriage requirements.

Fail-closed source-fidelity rejection. Chapter 5 defines abnormal-event checks as checks for crisis-avoidance action and safe landing while the event is occurring; this candidate strengthens that into a post-landing event-specific inspection duty that the cited source text does not explicitly state.
The source explicitly states that aircraft characteristics and operation method may require additional checks beyond the example list. This is a distinct process-design proposition.

Tier B PASS. The source explicitly makes registration-mark display a preflight inspection item. Q220/Q080 concern ongoing display/validity rather than the preflight go/no-go check; flight phase and decision boundary differ.
Tier B PASS. Chapter 5 explicitly includes pilot skill, flight experience and training status in preflight preparation. A valid certificate does not substitute for this mission-readiness check.

Tier B PASS. Chapter 5 explicitly requires checking aircraft certification validity and conditions/operating limitations in preflight preparation. Q226 tests legal operation beyond conditions; this item tests the preflight verification gate.
Helicopter takeoff lateral tendency from tail-rotor action, including direction depending on rotor rotation, is explicitly stated and is not already answer-defining in the canonical bank.

Tier B PASS. The source explicitly requires prompt climb out of the ground-effect range after helicopter takeoff. Q132 tests the ground-effect phenomenon; this item tests a source-defined takeoff action branch.
The source explicitly says to avoid rapid vertical climb except when unavoidable because rotor speed can decrease and the aircraft can become unstable.
Helicopter landing descent-rate reduction near the ground is an explicit source-defined touchdown-energy control and differs from VRS and post-touchdown rotor-safety questions.

Tier B PASS. The source explicitly says to avoid hovering within the ground-effect range and land promptly. Landing-phase action is materially different from general ground-effect recognition and takeoff-phase departure.
Fixed-wing takeoff power, climb-angle and stall-margin management are explicitly stated and form a distinct action sequence from runway-direction selection and generic stall physics.
Fixed-wing landing descent-rate reduction near the ground is explicit and distinct from the existing item about maintaining speed above stall and elevator control.

The source explicitly warns that visual-estimation error can cause runway excursion. This is a distinct landing consequence branch from runway-site physical-condition selection and generic manual distance training.

Chapter 5 explicitly permits combined operation in which aircraft flight is automatic while a camera or other payload is operated by a person. This is distinct from choosing manual versus automatic control for an entire task.

Tier B PASS. Chapter 5 explicitly states that failure of GNSS receivers, electronic compass or barometric sensors can require manual hazard avoidance. This is materially broader than GNSS-free operation alone and differs from the generic automatic-to-manual transition trigger.

Chapter 5.4.2 explicitly assigns assistants hazard-warning communication and guidance to an emergency landing point. This abnormal-state duty is distinct from normal third-party/access management and preflight coordination.

Tier B PASS. Chapter 5.4.2 explicitly includes aircraft recovery and safety-inspection assistance after landing. The post-landing lifecycle state and response sequence differ from normal in-flight assistant duties.
